claims.text: The variation in the link between social media use and adolescent mental health across developmental stages remains insufficiently clarified.
Social media use is significantly associated with worse mental health in school-aged youth (r = 0.308, 95%CI: 0.239–0.374, p < 0.001).
The meta-analytic association between social media use and adolescent mental health demonstrates high heterogeneity (I2 = 93.85%).
The association between social media use and mental health differs significantly across educational stages (Q = 9.72, p = 0.008).
The correlation between social media use and worse mental health is strongest in primary school students (r = 0.367).
The correlation between social media use and worse mental health is r = 0.334 in high school students.
The correlation between social media use and worse mental health is weakest in middle school students (r = 0.201).
No significant publication bias was detected in the meta-analysis.
The meta-analytic results were stable in leave-one-out sensitivity analysis.

evidence.description: Meta-analysis of twelve studies with 15 effect sizes found r = 0.308, 95%CI: 0.239–0.374, p < 0.001.
Heterogeneity testing yielded an I2 of 93.85%.
Subgroup stratification by educational stage showed Q = 9.72, p = 0.008.
Subgroup analysis yielded r = 0.367 for primary school students.
Subgroup analysis yielded r = 0.334 for high schoolers.
Subgroup analysis yielded r = 0.201 for middle schoolers.
Publication bias assessment detected no significant publication bias.
Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis confirmed that results were stable.

methodologies.name: Random-effects meta-analysis and subgroup stratification
methodologies.description: Systematic literature search and random-effects meta-analysis with subgroup stratification, heterogeneity testing, publication bias assessment, and leave-one-out sensitivity analysis performed using Stata 17.0.
conditions: Reported correlation coefficients between social media use and mental health in school-aged youth

limitations.text: The variation in the link between social media use and adolescent mental health across developmental stages remains insufficiently clarified in existing literature.

future_work.text: Development of developmentally tailored prevention and intervention strategies for school-aged youth.
